name: Ceramic braces
lead: Ceramic braces are fixed orthodontic appliances whose brackets are tooth-coloured rather than metal. They work like other fixed braces, using brackets, bonding material and an archwire to apply constant light pressure that moves teeth while new bone forms to support them in their new positions [7]. The payoff for appearance is twofold: straighter, better-aligned teeth at the end of treatment, and a less visible appliance along the way.

Aesthetic appliances are especially relevant to adults, who are described as demanding discreet options; a French questionnaire study of adult patients found the real need for treatment had no influence on the choice of an aesthetic appliance, and that the most demanding patients tended to be women in their thirties with professional jobs [4]. Ceramic braces and clear aligners are both described as cosmetic corrective devices compared with traditional metal braces [3].

Research includes comparisons of microbial adhesion on metal, ceramic and self-ligating brackets in vitro [2], surveys of how adults weigh aesthetics when choosing appliances [4], a study of appliance type and hiring prospects [3], and a 2025 comparison of oral-health-related quality of life with ceramic braces and aligners [8].

paras: A fixed brace has four traditional elements: brackets bonded to the teeth, bonding material, an archwire running through the brackets, and ligature elastics or similar fasteners that hold the wire in place [7]. In ceramic braces the brackets are made of a tooth-coloured material, so they blend with the teeth more than stainless-steel brackets do; the mechanics of tooth movement are the same as with other fixed appliances [7]. Wikipedia describes clear braces generally as nearly transparent and notes that cosmetic orthodontic options are more common in countries with first-world economies [7].

Ceramic and clear aligners are described as cosmetic options compared with traditional metallic braces [3]. Adult patients reportedly want discreet appliances, but the factors shaping their choice are still poorly understood [4].

Braces deliver constant light pressure on the teeth, and the bone around them remodels as the teeth shift [7]. Treatment typically lasts from six months to two and a half years depending on complexity, with adjustments about every three to six weeks, followed by retainers; Hawley, clear Essix and bonded wire retainers are the common types [7].

Wikipedia traces orthodontics through Pierre Fauchard's 1728 work on palate expansion, Christophe Delabarre's wire crib in 1819, the first article on orthodontics by Norman Kingsley in 1858, and Edward Angle's early twentieth-century classification system and orthodontic school [7]. Nitinol wires, developed at the Naval Ordnance Laboratory in 1959, were applied to treatment by George Andreasen in 1979 [7]. Tooth-coloured brackets belong to the later push for less visible appliances alongside lingual braces and clear aligners [3][4].

A cross-sectional study photographed two models with metal braces, ceramic braces and clear aligners and compared them with no appliance. Photographs were shown to 189 employers in Saudi Arabia, who rated professionalism, communication skills and likelihood of being hired. Scores for the models wearing metal and ceramic brackets were significantly lower than when they wore clear aligners or no appliance, and the authors concluded that appliances have cosmetic implications for hiring prospects [3].
A 2025 study compared oral-health-related quality of life in adults undergoing treatment with ceramic braces versus aligners [8].

Plaque, gingivitis and gum recession are common with fixed braces without careful cleaning, most patients experience some root resorption that is usually not clinically significant, and enamel decalcification is a recognised risk [7]. Fixed appliances are associated with increased Candida colonisation in a prospective controlled trial [1]. In vitro studies have examined biofilm formation on bracket types [2], salivary pH effects of different appliances [6], and enamel micro-cracks and debonding of ceramic brackets after thermocycling [5].

A prospective controlled trial found fixed orthodontic appliances change oral microbiota including Candida colonisation [1]. A cross-sectional employer survey examined appearance and hiring prospects with different appliances [3], a questionnaire study examined what adults weigh when choosing an aesthetic appliance [4], and a survey study compared quality of life with ceramic braces and aligners [8]. Other findings are laboratory-based [2][5][6].

card.summary: Tooth-coloured fixed braces that trade some visibility for the same bracket-and-wire mechanics.
card.note: Ceramic brackets differ from metal in debonding and enamel-stress laboratory findings.

quick.overview:
Ceramic braces use tooth-coloured brackets with a wire to straighten teeth, aiming to be less visible than metal.

Research is mostly surveys and lab studies.
quick.mechanism: Same as other fixed braces: steady wire pressure moves teeth as bone remodels.
quick.risks: Fixed appliances raise plaque and Candida colonisation; lab work examines enamel micro-cracks on debonding.

chain: Brackets and archwire apply steady light pressure
Teeth move and bone remodels around them
Tooth-coloured brackets keep the appliance less conspicuous during treatment
angle.text: Ceramic braces are used to straighten teeth and improve the smile like any fixed braces, while the tooth-coloured brackets make the appliance less noticeable than metal ones. Adults who want discreet treatment are a main market [4].
